section.title: Situation
section.p: The Strait of Hormuz is in acute crisis as of March 2026. Commercial traffic has fallen sharply — by mid-March, most shipping through the strait had halted, with only around 90 vessels observed crossing in a single snapshot period while the broader flow remained heavily disrupted. Iran's IRGC Navy maintains the principal local threat: fast attack craft, anti-ship cruise missiles, naval mines deployable from Ghadir-class submarines, drones, and shore-based sensors on controlled islands (Qeshm, Larak, Abu Musa, Greater and Lesser Tunbs). The US 5th Fleet operates escorts under Operation Epic Escort but was reported "not ready for weeks" to provide full tanker escort coverage at the crisis onset. War risk insurance premiums have spiked — the Joint War Committee has listed the strait as a high-risk area, and operators are delaying or withdrawing transits. Oil is above $120/bbl. Roughly one-fifth of the world's crude and a major share of global LNG transits this 21-nautical-mile- wide channel.

On the night of 23 March 2026, a projectile struck a gas pipeline feeding a power station in Khorramshahr, Khuzestan province — Iran's hydrocarbon heartland — further degrading an already war-stressed energy grid.
The question: could a private entity — not a state navy — open and secure the strait? Not as fantasy. As engineering.

subsection.title: 1. The Flying Tigers (1941–1942)
subsection.p: The American Volunteer Group: a private military air unit recruited from US service members, funded by the Chinese government, operating under the corporate front of CAMCO (Central Aircraft Manufacturing Company). They defended the Burma Road — a supply line — using 99 P-40 Warhawk fighters (100 ordered; one crate damaged in transit) against a larger Japanese air force. Legal status: contractors of a foreign government. Effective because they had the right equipment, experienced pilots, and a narrow mission (defend the road). Disbanded 4 July 1942 and absorbed into the 23rd Fighter Group, US Army Air Forces.
Lesson: A private force works when the mission is geographically constrained, the threat is definable, and a state sponsor provides legal cover and logistics.

subsection.title: 2. Operation Earnest Will (24 July 1987 – 26 September 1988)
subsection.p: The US reflagged 11 Kuwaiti tankers under the US registry, then escorted them through the Gulf with naval convoys. The first convoy hit a mine on 24 July 1987 — the tanker Bridgeton struck an Iranian mine on the operation's opening day. The USS Samuel B. Roberts hit a mine on 14 April 1988. Four days later, Operation Praying Mantis — the largest US naval engagement since World War II — destroyed the Iranian frigate Sahand, severely damaged the frigate Sabalan, sank the fast attack craft Joshan, and struck the Sirri and Sassan oil platforms.

The operation worked despite the mines because: convoy routing reduced exposure, mine countermeasures improved over time, and US retaliation imposed costs on Iran that exceeded the benefit of continued mining.

Lesson: Escort convoys work. Mines are the hardest problem. Routing discipline and operational security matter more than firepower. The political willingness to escalate — to destroy Iranian platforms and warships after the Roberts — was the actual deterrent, not the escorts themselves.

subsection.title: 3. Gulf of Aden Anti-Piracy (2008–2015)
subsection.p: Private armed security teams (PCASP) on merchant vessels effectively ended Somali piracy. The legal framework: IMO guidance MSC.1/Circ.1405/Rev.2 deferred to flag states, flag states authorized armed guards under varying national regimes, companies contracted private maritime security firms. The model was shipboard — teams of 3–4 armed guards per vessel, with escalating ROE (presence, warning, deterrent fire, protective fire). No merchant vessel carrying embarked armed guards was successfully hijacked during the suppression period. At the height of the crisis, several hundred embarked teams were operating simultaneously across the High Risk Area.

Lesson: Private maritime security works against asymmetric threats when the legal framework exists, flag states cooperate, and the threat model is well-understood. It does not work against state military forces. Somali pirates with RPGs and skiffs are not the IRGC Navy with C-802 anti-ship missiles.

section.title: Threat Model

section.p: Iran's A2/AD in the strait is layered. As of late March 2026, Operation Epic Fury has degraded many of these systems — IRGC claims 8,000+ targets struck, 60–120 fast attack craft sunk or combat-ineffective, ballistic missile and drone launch capacity down an estimated 90–95%. But the residual threat is the one that matters for a private operation, because mines do not need launchers and dispersed systems survive airstrikes.

def.desc: The primary threat and the one least affected by air campaigns. Iran is believed to possess thousands of naval mines including EM-52 rocket-propelled rising mines, SADAF-family bottom mines, and conventional moored contact mines. Deployable from submarines, surface craft, dhows, and even fishing boats. Covert minelaying in a busy commercial lane is nearly undetectable until the first ship hits one. No air campaign eliminates a mine already on the seabed.

Shore-based mobile launchers on the Iranian coast and island garrisons. Noor (C-802 derivative, ~120km, active radar terminal homing, sea-skimming, turbojet), Qader (~200km, extended-range Noor variant with inertial midcourse and active radar terminal), Khalij Fars (ballistic AShM, ~300km, terminal Mach 3–5 with electro-optical/radar seeker, Fateh-family derivative). Additionally, the Abu Mahdi cruise missile (~1,000km range, AI-guided, low-altitude, land/sea/air launch capable) entered serial production circa 2025. Many hardened coastal sites struck by 5,000-lb penetrators, but mobile transporter-erector-launchers survive by dispersion — the launchers that matter are the ones that moved before the strike.

IRGC Navy swarm doctrine. Pre-war strength: 100–200 armed speedboats including Ashura-class craft capable of 90+ km/h carrying Qadr heat-seeking missiles (25km range), Nasr-1 short-range AShM, RPGs, and mine-laying rails. Post–Epic Fury: 60–120+ sunk or combat-ineffective. The survivors are the ones hiding in coves and under bridges. In confined waters where maneuver space is limited, even a degraded swarm force creates ambiguity that degrades targeting confidence on both sides.

20+ Ghadir-class midget submarines (120-ton displacement, shallow-water optimized, difficult to track in the noisy Gulf thermocline). Armed with Hoot torpedoes, Nasr-1 missiles, and mine delivery capability. Some sunk in strikes. Fateh-class heavier submarines provide additional capability. The submarine threat is less about the weapons they carry and more about the uncertainty they create: a convoy that might be tracked by a submarine behaves differently than one that is not.

The fastest-evolving layer. Shahed-136 one-way attack drones (2,000+ km range, low-cost, mass-produced, tunnel-stored — launch capacity down 83–95% post-strikes but production continues). Mohajer-6/10 for reconnaissance and strike. Shahed-238 jet-powered variant for higher-speed attack. The 359 loitering surface-to-air system (150km range, unveiled January 2025) adds a new dimension: a loitering munition that hunts aircraft rather than ships. Iran used daily drone waves in the first week of the Gulf campaign. The drones are cheap enough to be expendable and numerous enough to saturate point defenses.

The kill chain begins here. Ghadir over-the-horizon radar for wide-area maritime and air surveillance. Sepehr OTH radar for detection and tracking. Electro-optical/infrared coastal observation posts on Qeshm, Abu Musa, Greater and Lesser Tunbs. AIS monitoring. Distributed ISR from islands and mainland creates persistent contact with all traffic in the strait. The advantage is not the individual sensor but the ability to find, fix, and track a ship long enough to coordinate a salvo. Some island sites (Abu Musa harbor, Tunbs installations) damaged by Epic Fury strikes; the degree of sensor degradation is not publicly confirmed.

The traffic separation scheme forces all shipping through a channel roughly 6 nautical miles wide: two-mile inbound lane, two-mile buffer, two-mile outbound lane. Iranian islands and coastline bracket the channel. Reaction time from shore to shipping lane is measured in minutes. The Musandam peninsula (Oman) provides the only non-Iranian coastline on the strait itself.

section.title: The Plan
section.p: A private operation to open Hormuz would require five capabilities that do not currently exist in any single private entity but could be assembled from existing commercial and quasi-commercial sources.

subsection.title: Phase 0: Legal Architecture
subsection.p: No private force can operate in an international strait without state sponsorship. The model is the Flying Tigers: a corporate entity chartered in a cooperating state. Oman is the obvious candidate — they control the Musandam peninsula, have a direct interest in strait access, and have historically maintained relations with both Iran and the West. The entity would operate under Omani flag, with Omani port access, under a bilateral security agreement.

Alternative sponsor: UAE (Fujairah is the bypass terminal and eastern terminus of the ADCOP — Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline — which can carry 1.5 million bbl/day, bypassing Hormuz entirely), but UAE participation would be read as alignment with the US/Israel coalition and eliminate diplomatic flexibility.

UNCLOS Part III, Article 38 establishes transit passage as a right in international straits used for international navigation. Iran has not ratified UNCLOS but the passage right is widely considered customary international law. The legal theory: the private entity enforces an existing right under contract to affected states and commercial interests.

subsection.title: Phase 1: Mine Countermeasures (the critical path)
subsection.p: Mines are the threat that makes everything else possible or impossible. A private MCM capability would need:

def.desc: Commercial AUVs can map and classify the seabed. The Kongsberg HUGIN family (including the HUGIN Endurance variant) is used by both commercial survey operators and defense customers. Saab's AUV62-MR mine reconnaissance system received a Swedish Navy order in 2024. The REMUS 600 (now under Kongsberg's portfolio after the Hydroid acquisition) is a medium-class UUV used for MCM and other payload missions. A fleet of 8–12 AUVs could survey the traffic separation scheme in 48–72 hours and maintain continuous re-survey on a rolling basis.

Side-scan and synthetic aperture sonar on the AUVs identifies mine-like objects. ATLAS ELEKTRONIK SeaCat can carry user-defined payloads in its flooded bow section and is registered as a dual-use good, exempt from ITAR restrictions. Thales SAMDIS is a compact sonar optimized for detecting naval mines, including in deeper waters.

This is the hardest commercial gap. Military mine disposal uses divers and expendable ROVs. ATLAS ELEKTRONIK's SeaFox is an expendable mine neutralizer — the vehicle is sent to the mine, confirms identification via camera, and detonates on contact. Some of these systems are available for export. A private operation would need either: (i) contracted military EOD teams from a participating state, (ii) commercial mine disposal ROVs operated under the Omani security agreement, or (iii) expendable autonomous mine neutralizers purchased from European defense firms (ATLAS ELEKTRONIK, Saab, ECA Group).

ATLAS ELEKTRONIK UK's ARCIMS USV platform can deploy and recover AUVs, tow mine sweeping gear, and maintain COLREGS-compliant autonomous navigation. A fleet of 6–8 USVs provides persistent MCM coverage without putting crews in the minefield.

subsection.p: The commercial MCM capability exists in pieces. Nobody has assembled it as a private service. The technology is mature. The integration is the gap.

subsection.title: Phase 2: Convoy Escort
subsection.p: The Operation Earnest Will model applied with private assets:

def.desc: Commercial offshore patrol vessels (60–80m class) equipped with naval guns (25–40mm), CIWS or similar point defense, decoys, and ESM. These vessels exist in the surplus naval market and the offshore security market. Crew them with ex-naval personnel under the Omani flag. A minimum of 4 escort vessels supports a daily convoy cycle.

Managed transit windows. Two convoys per day (one inbound, one outbound), timed to maximize separation and minimize exposure. Route selection varies daily. Speed governed by slowest vessel but minimum 10 knots through the strait.

The Gulf of Aden model scaled up. PCASP teams on every vessel in the convoy: 4–6 armed guards per ship, equipped for anti-swarm defense (heavy machine guns, anti-materiel rifles, shoulder-launched SAMs if the threat escalates to armed drones). Flag state authorization required per IMO MSC.1/Circ.1405/Rev.2.
Drone jamming, radar warning receivers, chaff/flare on escort vessels. Commercial maritime EW systems exist (Saab, Elbit, Rafael). This is the layer that makes the drone threat manageable.

Commercial satellite imagery (Planet, Maxar) for wide-area surveillance. AIS tracking (already commercial). Synthetic aperture radar satellites for all-weather vessel detection. Commercial providers can deliver near-real-time pictures of every vessel in the strait.

Long-endurance commercial drones (Textron Aerosonde, Schiebel Camcopter) operating from Musandam or Omani islands. Persistent overhead coverage of the convoy route. Radar and EO/IR payloads for surface search and periscope detection.

Deployable acoustic sensor arrays (commercial sonobuoy derivatives, seabed hydrophones) in the traffic separation scheme. Detects submarine and small craft movement. This technology exists commercially for offshore asset protection.

subsection.title: Phase 4: Defeating the Kill Chain (the missile problem)
subsection.p: The conventional framing says: cruise missiles are a state threat requiring a state response. A private force handles everything below the missile threshold and prays. This framing is wrong. It asks the question in the attacker's language. The question is not how do you intercept a Mach 3 missile? The question is how do you make the missile miss, or never launch?

A cruise missile needs a kill chain: detect, identify, track, target, engage, assess. The missile is the last link. A private entity cannot intercept the missile. But a private entity can break the kill chain at every other link.

def.desc: Commercial electronic warfare systems operating in reverse: radar spoofing, AIS manipulation, GPS-denied navigation for hostile sensors. The IRGC relies on shore-based radar (Qeshm, the Tunbs), maritime patrol aircraft, and fast attack craft with surface search radar. A private fleet carrying commercial ESM suites (Saab, Elbit, Rafael) can generate phantom contacts, mask real signatures, and degrade the targeting solution. Twelve radar returns where three ships transit. The seeker acquires a ghost. The technology is dual-use. The export controls are ambiguous. An Omani-flagged vessel carrying a commercial ECA electronic countermeasure suite is a survey ship with self-protection equipment.

The C-802 uses active radar terminal homing. The Khalij Fars uses imaging infrared or active radar at terminal phase. Both discriminate targets by radar cross section. Fill the 6-nautical-mile traffic separation scheme with radar reflectors: corner cubes on autonomous buoys, towed radar enhancer barges behind every convoy vessel at 500m offset, drone swarms carrying luneberg lenses. The radar cross section of the convoy becomes the radar cross section of the entire strait. The missile's terminal seeker sees a wall of returns and cannot discriminate. This is the chaff principle applied not to one ship but to the transit corridor. Commercial corner reflectors cost hundreds of dollars. Autonomous buoys cost thousands. The density required is a logistics problem, not a technology problem.

VLCCs spaced at maximum radar discrimination distance (the minimum range at which two targets of similar cross section merge into one return for the seeker — approximately 200-400m for a C-802 seeker at terminal range). OPV escorts positioned at the likely seeker acquisition bearings, carrying expendable decoys (chaff, flares, towed radar targets). Unmanned decoy barges in the threat axis — cheap, radar-bright, expendable. The formation is designed so that a missile acquiring at terminal phase hits the decoy, not the tanker. You are not intercepting the missile. You are making the missile miss by redesigning what the target looks like to a radar seeker at Mach 3.

Escort vessels still carry short-range air defense: CIWS or RAM equivalents for terminal intercept of subsonic cruise missiles and armed drones. This layer handles the C-802 (subsonic, sea-skimming) but not the Khalij Fars (Mach 3 ballistic). The point defense is not the primary defense. It is the last resort after deception, saturation, and formation have failed. A private entity can purchase CIWS. A private entity cannot purchase an integrated area air defense system. This remains the hard limit.

Iran has never fired a cruise missile at a commercial tanker. Not in the Tanker War (1984-1988). Not in Earnest Will. Not now. Iran mines, swarms with fast attack craft, seizes vessels, and shoots at military targets. A cruise missile into a VLCC carrying two million barrels of crude is an environmental catastrophe — Deepwater Horizon at sea, in the world's most important shipping lane. It turns every coastal state, every oil importer, and China (Iran's primary customer) against Tehran. The political cost exceeds the military value. The private entity does not need to make the missile technically impossible. It needs to make the political cost of firing it visible. Cameras on every vessel. Satellite feeds to every newsroom. A live-streamed transit corridor. The missile defense, in its highest form, is journalism.

subsection.p: The honest assessment: a private force cannot win a kinetic engagement against a state's cruise missile arsenal. But it does not need to. It needs to make the engagement unprofitable — technically (the missile misses), economically (the insurance math still works), and politically (the world is watching). The conventional framing treats the missile as a physics problem. The correct framing treats it as an information problem. The kill chain has six links. The missile is one. Break any other and the chain fails.

section.title: Cost Estimate

figure.alt: Fig. 4 — Economics of closure vs private security
figure.caption: Fig. 4 — Economics of closure vs private security

section.p: Rough order of magnitude for initial operating capability:

MCM fleet (12 AUVs, 8 USVs, disposal ROVs) $120M Escort vessels (4x OPV, armed/equipped) $200M ISR package (drones, satellites, sensors) $40M Shipboard security teams (100 operators) $15M/yr Personnel (crews, command, logistics) $80M/yr Omani basing and port services $30M/yr Insurance and legal $25M/yr Contingency and attrition $50M
Initial capital expenditure: ~$360M Annual operating cost: ~$150M/yr

For context: the insurance premium spike alone costs the shipping industry billions per year at crisis rates. A $150M/yr private security operation that reduces premiums back to pre-crisis levels pays for itself many times over. The ADCOP bypass pipeline can move 1.5M bbl/day but global transit through Hormuz in normal conditions exceeds 20M bbl/day. The bypass is a pressure valve, not a replacement. The economic incentive is overwhelming. The question is not cost. It is authority.

def.desc: A private MCM vessel that misses a mine, followed by a tanker explosion, creates a liability chain that no insurer will underwrite and no corporate entity will accept.

A private escort vessel that fires on an IRGC fast attack boat starts a war. Who authorized it? Under whose rules of engagement? The Flying Tigers worked because they were fighting Japan, not harassing it. The ambiguity of the Hormuz situation — neither peace nor declared war — makes private ROE impossible to define without state backing.

The international order assumes that only states secure waterways. UNCLOS assigns responsibility to littoral states. A private force, no matter how capable, operates in a legal void unless a state claims it.

Iran would treat a private escort force as a proxy. The diplomatic fiction ("it's not a state navy, it's a commercial security service") would last until the first engagement. After that it is a belligerent.

section.title: What Would Actually Work
section.p: The plan that has historical support and legal viability is a hybrid: the Gulf of Aden model for shipboard security, the Earnest Will model for state escort, and commercial autonomous MCM to fill the mine clearance gap. Specifically:

item.p: An Omani-flagged commercial MCM service, operating autonomous AUVs and USVs to survey and clear the traffic separation scheme. This is commercially viable, legally defensible under Omani sovereignty, and fills a real gap — the US Navy's MCM readiness was publicly reported as inadequate for immediate escort duties at the crisis onset, and the UK mine hunter fleet (Hunt-class, Sandown-class) has shrunk through decommissionings and delayed recapitalization.
Expanded PCASP on every vessel transiting the strait, funded by a shared industry levy (like the Gulf of Aden model). This deters fast boat harassment and drone attacks at the ship level.

State naval escort for high-value convoy windows, provided by any combination of US, UK, French, Indian, Pakistani, or GCC navies. This provides the air defense umbrella and the political deterrent against cruise missile attack. The International Maritime Security Construct (IMSC), already operating in the region, provides a multilateral framework for coordination.
A commercial maritime domain awareness service providing real-time ISR to all convoy participants via satellite, drone, and sensor fusion. This is a SaaS product, not a military operation.

section.p: The guerrilla insight is that the most militarily effective component — mine clearance — is also the most commercially viable and the least politically provocative. An Omani company operating robots that find and destroy mines is not a mercenary navy. It is a marine services contractor. The mines do not care who finds them. The insurance markets do not care who clears them. The legal framework for commercial mine survey already exists in the offshore energy sector.

The $360M capital cost buys a capability that no state navy currently has at the required scale and responsiveness. Commercial autonomous MCM — operated by a private entity, funded by shipping industry levies, based in Oman — could be the thing that actually opens the strait, while the state navies handle the parts of the problem that require sovereignty.

item.p: Would Oman agree? Their balancing act between Iran and the West is the foundation. A private MCM service operating from Musandam would need to be framed as Omani national interest, not as a Western proxy.
Who funds the capital expenditure? Lloyd's, the P&I clubs, the major tanker operators (NITC excluded), sovereign wealth funds of transit-dependent states (Japan, South Korea, India)?
Can commercial AUVs actually find Iranian mines in operational conditions — current, silt, shallow water, acoustic clutter? The technology works in exercises. Exercises are not wars.
What happens when Iran sinks an unmanned survey vessel? Is that an act of war? Against whom? The robot has no flag state feelings.

The precedent problem: if a private entity secures Hormuz, who secures Malacca? Bab el-Mandeb? The Panama Canal? The model either scales or it doesn't. If it scales, the international maritime order changes. If it doesn't, Hormuz is a one-off that proves the rule.
